                     ANN MEWHINNEY MATOUS’ INITIAL BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       Intervenor Ann Mewhinney Matous, individually, and as representative of Kate Richter

Brown, Suzanna Richter, Mary Mewhinney Smith, Madison Goodman, Connor Smith, Miranda

Smith, the Ann Mewhinney Irrevocable Ranch Trust 2024, the Mary Mewhinney Irrevocable

Ranch Trust 2025, and Cathey Creek Limited (collectively, the “Mewhinney Family”), files this

Initial Brief to the Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission

Services Corporation (“Applicants”) to Amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity

for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project

(“Application”) in the above referenced docket, and shows as follows:

                                      INTRODUCTION

       The Mewhinney Family respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”)

recommend that the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) deny the Application,

as the evidentiary record does not demonstrate compliance with the requirements of Public Utility

                                               1
 Regulatory Act (“PURA”) Section 37.056 and 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) Section

25.101. Despite the unprecedented scale and consequences of the proposed project, the Applicants

have failed to present the type of complete, route-specific, and evidence-based showing that the

statute and Commission rules require as a condition of authorization to construct a major

transmission facility, let alone part of the first 765-kV project ever constructed in Texas.

       PURA Section 37.056 and 16 TAC Section 25.101 delineate the criteria that the

Commission must utilize when determining whether to issue a Certificate of Convenience and

Necessity (“CCN”) for construction of a new transmission line. Prior to approving an application,

the Commission must assess the statutory factors, including the adequacy of the existing service,

the need for additional service, the effect of the proposed transmission infrastructure on

landowners and the environment, the impact on community values and recreational and park areas,

and the effects on historical and aesthetic resources. Additionally, the Commission must ensure

that the routing of proposed infrastructure appropriately balances these competing considerations.

These statutory and regulatory requirements are designed to guarantee that transmission projects

receive approval only when applicants demonstrate that their proposals are justified, suitably

designed, and aligned with the public interest.

       The Applicants, not the Commission or the intervenors, bear the burden to make this

showing. As the applicants seeking permission to construct the first 765-kV transmission line in

Texas, cutting across hundreds of miles of private property, including ecologically sensitive areas

such as the iconic Colorado River and Texas state parks, the Applicants must establish that the

project satisfies the statutory considerations set forth in PURA and Commission rules. Yet, the

evidence presented in this proceeding does not sufficiently demonstrate that the Application

adequately addresses, much less satisfies, the full range of statutory and regulatory factors the



                                                  2
 Commission is required to consider, including need, environmental integrity, aesthetic values,

costs, and impacts to landowners and communities. In several respects, the lack of route-specific

information and accurate data prevent a meaningful evaluation of those statutory and regulatory

factors. Because the Commission may grant a CCN only when the requirements of PURA Section

37.056 are satisfied, and because the record here does not establish that those requirements have

been met, the Application should be denied.

       If the ALJs do not recommend denial of the Application, the Mewhinney Family urges the

ALJs to recommend selection of Route 392 as the route that “best meets” the requirements of

PURA Section 37.056 (c)(4)(A)-(D) and 16 TAC Section 25.101(b)(3)(B). Compared to other

recommended routes, Route 392 has similar cost metrics and only a small number of additional

habitable structures, but performs superiorly on all of the other important statutory factors,

including environmental integrity, community values, aesthetic values, and paralleling compatible

right-of-way (“ROW”). Critically, unlike the Applicants and PUC staff engineer’s recommended

Routes 894 and 487, Route 392 avoids creating a new transmission line crossing in a currently

pristine area of the Colorado River, an environmentally and aesthetically sensitive feature of the

Texas landscape, and avoids impacts to nearby Colorado Bend State Park. Rather, Route 392

utilizes Link U3, the only link crossing the Colorado River that runs parallel to an existing

electrical transmission line.

       Furthermore, the Mewhinney Family also opposes any route using the newly added Link

C4, including Route 894 and Route 487, the routes identified by Applicants and Commission staff

as the “best meets” route, respectively. Contrary to PURA and Commission rules, Link C4 does

not follow compatible ROWs, instead fragmenting family-owned ranches and private property.

Landowners on Link C4, such as the Mewhinney Family, also suffered an extreme disadvantage



                                                3
 in this proceeding compared to landowners on preliminary route links who received notice and

had the opportunity to provide important input on this project at public meetings in June 2025,

more than one year before landowners on newly added links, such as Link C4, received notice of

this massive project. For these reasons, should the ALJs decide to recommend approval of the

Application, the Mewhinney Family respectfully urges the recommendation of Route 392.

                                        BACKGROUND

       On March 26, 2026, Applicants filed their Application for a proposed transmission line

pursuant to 16 TAC Section 25.174 to construct, own, and operate the Bell County East Switch to

Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell,

Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green,

and Williamson Counties (“Transmission Line Project”).1 Applicants included 122 alternative

transmission line routes in the Application, which it grouped into five geographic corridors

identified as: (1) the northern corridor using Link U6; (2) the central corridor using Link J12; (3)

the central corridor using Link J27; (4) the central corridor using Link J24; and (5) the southern

corridor using Link J32.2 Out of the 122 identified alternative routes, Applicants ultimately

selected Route 8943 of the Link J27 corridor routes as the route that best meets the requirements

of PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and 16 TAC Section 25.101(b)(3)(B).4 Commission staff

engineer John Poole identified Route 487 as the best meets route.5

       Almost one year prior to filing the Application, the Applicants conducted public outreach

to gather community input on the Transmission Line Project. The Applicants held public meetings

                                              ARGUMENT

A.      The Applicants have failed to meet their burden under PURA and Commission rules
        to justify approval of the Transmission Line Project.

        1.      Applicants have not met their burden to establish need for the Transmission
                Line Project.

        Under PURA Section 37.056, the Applicants bear the burden of proving the need for the

Transmission Line Project. See PURA § 37.056(c)(2); 30 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A). Although the

Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”) has recommended the Transmission Line Project

as part of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”), that alone does not establish that the

requisite burden has been met. The Commission must independently determine whether the

Applicants have met the statutory requirements to demonstrate the need for the proposed

Transmission Line Project.

         The record consistently demonstrates that the PBRP remains actively contested. American

Stewards of Liberty’s (“ASL”) Motion to Defer Determination of Need identifies the following

contested questions: whether ERCOT evaluated reasonable alternatives to the Transmission Line

Program; whether additional generation located close to the Permian Basin load could reduce or

eliminate the need for Transmission Line Project; whether ERCOT assumed continued separation

between generation and load; whether local generation alternatives were adequately evaluated; and

whether transmission expansion was predetermined by the modeling assumptions utilized in the

PBRP.18 These concerns have not only been brought up by the ASL, but by the Commission itself.

The Commission’s procedural treatment of related proceedings demonstrates the question of need

remains unresolved. In Docket No. 59182, the ALJs determined that the Proposal for Decision

would reserve the issue of need for determination in this Docket No. 59475.19 This approach

illustrates that the ALJs recognized that need presents a threshold issue arising from the broader

PBRP and should be considered to the fullest.

        Additionally, Texas legislators have recently questioned the need for 765-kV transmission

lines and the PBRP more broadly. In the Brief of Certain Texas Legislators, Texas legislators

explain that the assumptions underlying the PBRP remain disputed.20 The legislators do not

provide route-specific evidence and instead discuss: whether the PBRP sufficiently evaluated

alternatives; whether the Transmission Line Project is the most cost-effective solution; and

whether local generation alternatives received adequate consideration. While these statements do

not alone establish any factual proposition, they further illustrate that legislative interpretations

        The Commission must determine whether the Applicants have proven the necessity of the

Transmission Line Project, not whether the Transmission Line Project is generally desirable.

Where the underlying planning assumptions remained disputed, where reasonable alternatives

        For these reasons, the Mewhinney Family respectfully urges the ALJs to recommend that

transmission facilitates as proposed.

        2.       The Transmission Line Project does not align with community values.

through which it would pass. PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(A) requires consideration of the impacts

of granting Applicants’ Transmission Line Project on community values. While “community

values” is not defined in statute or rule, the Commission interprets it as “a shared appreciation of

an area or other natural resource by members of a national, regional, or local community.”22

Adverse effects on community values are those that significantly alter the use, enjoyment, or

intrinsic value attached to an important area.23 Protecting community values is essential to ensuring

        The record demonstrates that the Transmission Line Project will have widespread and

substantial adverse impacts on community values. To solicit opinions on community values,

Applicants held three public meetings in June 2025, as described above, at which it gathered public

feedback on the project.24 The public comments reflect broad and consistent concerns that the

proposed transmission line would adversely affect community values across multiple dimensions.

These concerns include impacts to fish and wildlife, endangered species, environmental resources,

agricultural and ranching operations, residences, historic and cultural sites, property values, public

health, aesthetics, flood protection, and river features.25 Landowners also emphasized the

cumulative burden of existing infrastructure in some areas and the resulting strain on rural land

use and quality of life.26 The record reflects widespread opposition grounded in the belief that the

project would significantly disrupt established land uses and community character across the

affected corridor. The unprecedented level of participation and opposition to the Transmission

Line Project at the hearing on the merits in this proceeding, confirms the massive impact on

community values in general.

        Although Link C4 was added at the last minute, the community of Holland, Texas came

together to dispute the Transmission Line Project and submitted 224 protests and interventions for

Link C4 within a three-week period, each specifically noting that that proposed transmission line

would adversely affect their community values. With a population of approximately 1,300

residents, Holland received input from a number of individuals equivalent to 17% of the total town

population. This record shows there would be a significant community impact if the project

        Even within the concerns that the record reflects, there remains an additional limitation:

the lack of real-world precedent for a 765-kV transmission line in Texas. That absence of

operational experience further constrains the ability of both Applicants and the Commission to

fully evaluate the magnitude and nature of potential community impacts associated with the

project. Accordingly, the Application fails to satisfy the requirements of PURA Section 37.056

and should be denied.

        3.      The Transmission Line Project would result in excessive land fragmentation.

        The Application should be denied based on the Transmission Line Project’s excessive,

substantial, and unprecedented land fragmentation across a large portion of Central Texas. Rather

than maximizing and utilizing existing ROWs, the Transmission Line Project would result in land

fragmentation across a large swath of the state, with vast impacts to private property, and in

particular, rural Texas ranches with agricultural properties. In determining whether to approve a

transmission line project, Commission rules require consideration of whether the routes parallel or

utilize existing compatible rights-of-way and whether a proposed route minimizes adverse impacts

to the affected community and landowners. 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). Former Commissioner

Barry Smitherman expressed concerns about the Application on the basis of excessive land

 fragmentation, among other problems. He testified, “the Application has very limited instances

with links that follow existing transmission lines or other compatible rights-of-way, or property

lines as opposed to further fragmentation of habitat and properties. This approach is contrary to

the commonly held value in this state that we try to preserve large parcels of land to promote land

stewardship.”28 As proposed, the Transmission Line Project would result in excessive and

egregious land fragmentation and the ALJs should recommended denial of the Application.

        4.       The Applicants rely on speculative cost estimates that do not support project
                 approval.

        The Application contains speculative, and unproven, cost estimates that do not support

approval of the Transmission Line Project. Commission rules require the consideration of project

costs in making transmission line routing decisions. See 16 TAC § 22.101(b)(3)(B). However, the

evidentiary record confirms that the cost estimates provided by Applicants are conceptual,

preliminary, and subject to substantial uncertainty, including but not limited to on foot surveying,

geotechnical investigations, subsurface utility engineering, and detailed engineering analysis

based on the foregoing. Applicants therefore cannot identify with certainty the actual costs

associated with any proposed route, making this metric unsuitable for reliance for Commission

approval of the Application, without additional information. This deficiency is particularly

problematic for newly added links that were not among preliminary alternative route links, such

as Link C4.

        Applicants have never constructed a 765-kV transmission line and cannot verify their cost

numbers with any degree of certainty or provide any margin of error.29 Throughout discovery, the

Applicants acknowledge that their estimates do not incorporate site-specific design, which can

        Routes with newly added links, such as Link C4, suffer from additional cost uncertainty.

The Applicants had over a year to determine more precise cost estimates for originally proposed

route links presented to the public in June 2025, yet, the Application still fails to provide cost

with newly added links have even more cost uncertainty, as such routes did not have the benefit

evaluate the costs associated with the project and the route alternatives.

Transmission Line Project as proposed. As former Commissioner Mr. Smitherman testified, “This

B.         Should the ALJs recommend approval of the Transmission Line Project, Route 392
           better aligns with the factors set forth in PURA Section 37.056(c) and 16 TAC

           The Mewhinney Family supports Route 392, as a route that meets the overall community

values and best addresses the requirements of PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and 16 TAC

Section 25.101(b)(3)(B) compared to the other alternative routes in the Application. PURA Section

37.056(c)(4) requires the Commission to consider the effect of its decision on a new transmission

line project on community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values,

environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of costs to

consumers. In addition, the Commission’s rule Section 25.101(b)(3)(B) requires that, in approving

a route, the Commission consider the transmission line project’s engineering constraints, costs,

moderation of impact on the affected community and landowners, paralleling, and prudent

avoidance.

           Based     on    a   comprehensive       comparison,      Route     392    better   satisfies       PURA

Section 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D)’s and 16 TAC Section 25.101(b)(3)(B)’s criteria than either Route

894 or Route 487. Route 392 has similar cost metrics, only a small number of additional habitable

structures, but performs superiorly on other important metrics, including environmental integrity

and aesthetic values, paralleling compatible ROW, and avoids creating a new crossing in a

 currently pristine area of the Colorado River, an environmentally and aesthetically sensitive feature

of the Texas landscape. As confirmed by multiple experts in the proceeding, the avoidance of

creating a new crossing of the Colorado River offers a clear, bright line metric that sets Route 392

apart from the other recommended routes, and that does not suffer from flaws inherent in the

Application’s other metrics, including speculative cost estimates and inaccurate habitable structure

counts. Multiple highly respected experts, including former Commissioner Barry Smitherman,

former Executive Director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department Andrew Sansom, and many

others, advocate against approving a route that crosses the Colorado River at a pristine crossing

location – a flaw present in both Route 894 (Link J22) and Route 487 (Link J11). Collectively,

weighing the statutory and regulatory factors holistically, Route 392 stands above the other 121

alternative routes offered by the Applicants in this proceeding.

         1.       Environmental integrity favors Route 392. (PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(D)).

         As the record evidence makes clear, including in testimony by multiple highly experienced

expert witnesses, Route 392 performs superiorly over Route 894 with regard to environmental

integrity. Unlike Routes 894 and 487, Route 392 avoids causing environmental impacts to a

pristine section of the Colorado River. Multiple experts have identified the use of an existing

crossing corridor as environmentally superior to other routes.34

         From the perspective of environmental integrity, a route utilizing an existing ROW across

a river performs superiorly when compared to a route that creates an entirely new river crossing.

Route 894 contains Link J22 and Route 487 contains Link J11, which both cross the Colorado

        The environmental impacts of a new crossing of the Colorado River are significant and

include vegetation clearing, disturbance to soil and habitat, and potential disruption of ecological

connectivity, which can alter the character of the river corridor and affect both wildlife and human

use of the area.37 According to expert Andrew Sansom, who previously served as the Executive

Director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department: “These impacts are not limited to the

immediate crossing point. They can extend into the surrounding environment through the creation

of access routes, clearing of right-of-way, and long-term maintenance activities, all of which can

affect the broader landscape.”38 In contrast, “[c]onfining infrastructure impacts to a single river

crossing location, where feasible, reduces the overall footprint of disturbance and helps preserve

the surrounding environment.”39 Accordingly, former Commissioner Smitherman testified, “the

Commission should avoid approving a crossing of the Colorado River at a previously undisturbed

area.”40 Thus, environmental integrity strongly supports recommendation of Route 392 over other

options.
